I first read the current default calibration of the real Garnet computer (calibration set 9069c4ef-7ab6-4e50-be4f-c91d71c3a06d). It lists 30 qubit pairs that can run a CZ gate. Each pair has an IRB fidelity. IRB fidelity measures how often the CZ gate does the right thing. I checked every chain of 3 qubits a-b-c where both a-b and b-c are CZ pairs. The best chain is QB7-QB12-QB11, with QB12 in the middle. The QB7-QB12 fidelity is 0.99907. The QB12-QB11 fidelity is 0.99945. Their product is 0.99852. The next best chain scored 0.99818.

Next I ran a 3-qubit GHZ circuit on exactly QB7, QB12, and QB11 on garnet:mock with 200 shots. The job ID is 01a16486-a3f8-7266-833d-5c5da393efcf. I read the circuit back from the server. It has 2 CZ gates, one on QB12-QB7 and one on QB12-QB11. It measures all 3 qubits. The circuit puts QB12 into an equal mix of 0 and 1. Then it copies that value onto QB7 and QB11.

The counts were 000: 53, 011: 61, 100: 41, 111: 45. In each bitstring the rightmost bit is QB7, the middle bit is QB12, and the leftmost bit is QB11. A perfect quantum computer would give only 000 and 111, about 100 times each. The mock backend does not simulate the circuit. It returns random-looking counts, so these numbers do not show entanglement. They only show that the job ran and that the server accepted the circuit on the chosen qubits.

The principle is that a GHZ state links the qubits. All three qubits read 0 together or 1 together. To see this on hardware, you need the real garnet computer, not the mock. Picking the chain with the best CZ fidelities gives the GHZ state the best chance to survive the gate errors. The mock job used 0 credits.
